solution.concept_anchor: Dagh system — branding horses to prevent fraud
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is deceptive because maintaining a register of horse ownership sounds administratively identical to branding, leading students unfamiliar with the physical enforcement mechanism to choose it.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Dagh involved branding horses, not soldiers — physical marks on soldiers describe Chehra-adjacent thinking, not Dagh.
Eliminate option (c): maintaining a paper ownership register describes a documentary measure, not the physical branding mechanism of Dagh.
Eliminate option (d): Dagh was about horses presented at muster, not camels or war elephants — scope-extension trap.
Confirm option (b): Dagh mandated the physical branding of cavalry horses so that inferior or borrowed animals could not be substituted during inspection.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students often confuse Dagh with Chehra because both combat fraud. Dagh specifically targeted horses — fraudulent substitution of inferior animals before muster inspections. A student who has only partially studied the system may conflate the physical branding of horses with the descriptive roll of soldiers (Chehra), choosing option (a) or (c). The key discriminator is that Dagh was a mark burned onto the animal, not a paper record.
solution.final_explanation:
Alauddin Khilji introduced the Dagh (branding) system to eliminate the practice of soldiers presenting hired or inferior horses during military musters. Each cavalry horse was physically branded, creating a permanent identifier tied to its registered owner-soldier.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Physical marking of soldiers is the domain of Chehra (descriptive rolls), not Dagh. Conflating the two is the classic trap.
• Option (b) — Correct: Dagh required mandatory branding of horses to prevent fraudulent substitution of inferior animals at inspection.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Maintaining paper ownership registers was a documentary supplement, not the defining mechanism of Dagh.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Dagh system applied specifically to cavalry horses; camels and elephants are a scope extension.

Value Addition:
• Dagh and Chehra together formed Alauddin's twin anti-fraud pillars — Dagh for horses, Chehra for soldiers.
• The Diwan-i-Arz (military department) administered both systems under the Ariz-i-Mumalik.
• Without the Dagh system, the cash salary-based army could not be efficiently maintained as soldiers would claim pay for horses they did not possess.

solution.concept_anchor: Dagh vs. Chehra — distinct anti-fraud instruments

statement_analysis.statement: The Chehra system maintained physical descriptive records of individual soldiers to prevent impersonation and 'dead pay' fraud.
statement_analysis.reason: Chehra was a roll recording the physical appearance of each soldier so that dead or absent soldiers could not continue to draw pay through imposters.

statement_analysis.statement: The Dagh system served the same administrative purpose as Chehra, differing only in that it applied to soldiers rather than horses.
statement_analysis.reason: Dagh targeted horse substitution fraud (branding animals), while Chehra targeted soldier identity fraud — their targets and mechanisms were entirely distinct, not merely applied to different subjects.

statement_analysis.statement: Both Dagh and Chehra were administered through the Diwan-i-Arz under Alauddin Khilji.
statement_analysis.reason: The military department (Diwan-i-Arz) headed by the Ariz-i-Mumalik was the institutional home of both anti-fraud mechanisms, requiring a strengthened bureaucratic apparatus.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) tempts students who know Statements 1 and 3 are correct and assume Statement 2 must also be correct because Dagh and Chehra do share the same department and anti-fraud purpose.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 correct: Chehra recorded physical descriptions of soldiers — this is its defining feature distinguishing it from Dagh.

Identify Statement 2 as incorrect: the trap here is subtle — Dagh and Chehra did NOT serve the same purpose applied to different subjects; Dagh targeted animal fraud, Chehra targeted personal identity fraud.
Confirm Statement 3 correct: both systems functioned under Diwan-i-Arz — this is well-established.
Since Statements 1 and 3 are correct and Statement 2 is incorrect, select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap here is sophisticated: a partially prepared student who knows both systems were anti-fraud tools under the same department may conclude they were the same thing applied differently. Statement 2 exploits this by framing Dagh as 'Chehra for horses.' The correct understanding is that the fraud they combated was categorically different — Chehra addressed who (the soldier), Dagh addressed what (the horse).
solution.final_explanation:
Alauddin's military reforms included two distinct but complementary anti-fraud systems. Understanding their differences is critical for UPSC.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Chehra was a descriptive roll recording each soldier's physical appearance, preventing 'dead pay' fraud where salaries were drawn for soldiers who had died or deserted.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: This statement incorrectly equates Dagh with Chehra by suggesting they serve the same purpose for different subjects. Dagh was about branding horses to detect animal substitution; Chehra was about recording soldiers to detect impersonation — fundamentally different frauds.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Both Dagh and Chehra were administered under the Diwan-i-Arz, which required significant bureaucratic expansion under Alauddin.

Value Addition:
• Ariz-i-Mumalik was the head of Diwan-i-Arz — distinct from Wazir who headed Diwan-i-Wizarat.
• Together these systems anticipated modern HR and asset-management functions in military administration.
• Barani credits both systems as uniquely Alauddin's innovations with no precedent in earlier sultanate governance.

solution.concept_anchor: Standing army reform — iqta impact and cash salary

statement_analysis.statement: Alauddin Khilji's shift to a centrally paid standing army entirely abolished the iqta system, which was thereafter replaced by direct treasury grants.
statement_analysis.reason: The iqta system as an institution was NOT abolished; Alauddin curtailed the military autonomy of iqta holders but continued using iqtas for provincial revenue administration.

statement_analysis.statement: Under Alauddin's naqdi (cash salary) reform, soldiers were paid directly from the imperial treasury, reducing dependence on iqtadar intermediaries for military recruitment.
statement_analysis.reason: The naqdi system was precisely the mechanism by which Alauddin decoupled military recruitment from iqtadar obligations, with pay flowing directly from the state treasury.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Both incorrect — tempts students who recall that Alauddin did restrict iqtas and may over-generalise to conclude Statement 2 is also incorrect because it implies iqtadars had no role at all.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The word 'entirely abolished' makes this incorrect — Alauddin weakened iqtadar military power but retained iqtas for provincial administration.
Evaluate Statement 2: Naqdi (cash salary) paid directly from treasury is historically accurate — this statement is correct.
Since only Statement 1 is NOT correct, select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 1 uses 'entirely abolished' — a common UPSC trap that takes a partially true fact (iqtas were weakened) and extends it falsely to total abolition. Students who know Alauddin drastically curtailed iqta autonomy may accept the statement without catching the word 'entirely.'
solution.final_explanation:
Alauddin's creation of a standing army was one of the most consequential military reforms in Delhi Sultanate history, but it is frequently misunderstood in its relationship to the iqta system.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Alauddin did NOT abolish iqtas. He reduced the military dimension of iqtadars — they could no longer raise private armies from their revenue assignments — but the iqta remained the backbone of provincial administration. The 'entirely abolished' claim is the trap.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The naqdi system meant soldiers received cash salaries directly from the imperial treasury. This was revolutionary because it made the soldier's loyalty run to the Sultan, not to a local military lord.

Value Addition:
• Iltutmish and Balban relied heavily on iqtadars for military manpower — Alauddin broke this dependence.
• The naqdi system required a large, reliable revenue base — funded partly by enhanced land revenue (half of produce) and Deccan spoils.
• Firuz Shah Tughlaq reversed this by restoring hereditary military service and jagirs, showing how fragile the reform was institutionally.

solution.concept_anchor: Salary-price control interdependence in Alauddin's army

statement_analysis.statement: Infantry soldiers under Alauddin received approximately 78 tankas per year while cavalry soldiers received approximately 234 tankas per year.
statement_analysis.reason: Barani records these approximate salary figures — infantry at 78 tankas and cavalry at 234 tankas annually — reflecting the deliberate differential between arms.

statement_analysis.statement: The low salary policy was primarily a measure to reduce the size of the army and keep military expenditure manageable.
statement_analysis.reason: The low salary policy was designed to maintain a LARGE army affordably — it was not a size-reduction measure but a fiscal strategy made viable by keeping commodity prices artificially low through market controls.

statement_analysis.statement: Alauddin's salary policy and his market reforms were structurally interdependent — the collapse of one would undermine the other.
statement_analysis.reason: When Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah dismantled market controls after Alauddin's death, the low salaries could no longer sustain soldiers' living standards, causing the system's collapse — confirming the structural interdependence.

statement_analysis.statement: Ibn Battuta and Barani both noted that the salary-price control system remained robust and was continued by Alauddin's immediate successors.
statement_analysis.reason: Both sources indicate the system collapsed after Alauddin — Barani describes deregulation under Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah as causing the army's unsustainability, directly contradicting this statement.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Only two correct — tempts students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 3 but mistakenly believe Statement 2 or 4 is also valid, particularly Statement 4 which names two authoritative historical sources.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Salary figures of 78 tankas (infantry) and 234 tankas (cavalry) are from Barani — accept as correct.
Statement 2: 'Reduce the size of the army' is factually wrong — the low salary was designed to EXPAND army size affordably — eliminate.
Statement 3: The interdependence of salary and market reform is historically documented through the post-Alauddin collapse — accept as correct.
Statement 4: Both Barani and Ibn Battuta indicate the system collapsed after Alauddin, not continued — eliminate.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct, so the answer is option (a): Only one... wait — two statements are correct, so option (b) Only two. Recheck: correct answer is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 is a plausible-fabrication trap using authoritative source names (Ibn Battuta and Barani) to lend credibility to a false claim. Students who have encountered these names in their reading may accept the statement without recalling that both sources actually document the system's failure after Alauddin, not its continuation.
solution.final_explanation:
Alauddin's salary structure was not an isolated policy — it was the demand side of a two-sided system whose supply side was artificial price control across four regulated markets.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Infantry at ~78 tankas/year and cavalry at ~234 tankas/year per Barani. The cavalry-infantry differential also reflected the greater cost of maintaining horses.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The low salary policy was designed to sustain a LARGE army, not reduce it. With grain, cloth, and livestock priced far below market rates, soldiers' real purchasing power was maintained despite low nominal salaries.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The system was structurally codependent. The moment Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah deregulated markets, the low salaries became genuinely inadequate, and the large army became fiscally unsustainable.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Both Barani and Ibn Battuta document the system's collapse after Alauddin, not its continuation by successors.

Value Addition:
• This interdependence is a rare example of integrated fiscal-military policy in medieval India.
• Muhammad bin Tughlaq tried to maintain army size without price controls — the resulting fiscal crisis contributed to his policy chaos.
• UPSC frequently tests whether students understand WHY Alauddin's reforms were unique and WHY they could not outlast him.

solution.concept_anchor: Barani's army figures — source criticism and exaggeration
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Barani is the primary source and that the army was indeed very large may accept both A and R as correct and assume R explains A without testing the causal link.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Barani did record approximately 475,000 soldiers, and historians do debate these numbers as likely exaggerated. A is factually correct.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Alauddin did fund his army substantially through Deccan campaign revenues and enhanced land revenue. R is factually correct.

Step 3: Does R explain A? — The revenue sources (R) explain HOW the army was funded, not WHY Barani's figures are considered exaggerated. The exaggeration concern (A) arises from source criticism of Barani's methodology, not from fiscal capacity. R does not causally explain A.
A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is reversed-causation: students may assume that because Alauddin had large revenues (R), a large army figure makes sense, and therefore R explains A. But A is about the credibility of Barani's numerical claims — a historiographical issue — while R is about fiscal sources. A historian doubts 475,000 because of Barani's general tendency to exaggerate, not because the revenue base was insufficient. These are separate analytical dimensions.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests the intersection of military history and source criticism — an important UPSC angle.

Assertion (A): Historians, including many contemporary medievalists, question Barani's figure of 475,000 soldiers as likely inflated. Barani wrote during Firuz Shah's reign and may have amplified Alauddin's achievements for literary effect. A is correct.

Reason (R): Alauddin's fiscal base — enhanced land revenue (reportedly half of produce), Deccan spoils, and confiscated noble wealth — was real and substantial. R is correct.

Causal link: R does not explain A. The reason Barani's figures are doubted is not that the revenue was insufficient but that Barani as a source has historiographical limitations (hagiographic tendencies, writing decades after events). The fiscal capacity (R) is a separate issue from source reliability (A).

Correct answer: (b) — Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

Value Addition:
• Amir Khusrau's Khaza'in-ul-Futuh is a contemporary but laudatory source — hagiographic bias must be discounted.
• Archaeological evidence (Siri fort remains, monetised coin hoards) helps corroborate textual accounts.
• UPSC Mains increasingly tests this 'what sources say vs. what they omit' dimension of medieval historiography.

formatted_presentation.display_text:

solution.concept_anchor: Mongol battles — chronological sequence under Alauddin
solution.strong_distractor: b — This option places Kili before Jalandhar, which feels plausible since Kili is more famous, leading students to rank battles by prominence rather than date.
elimination_logic: The Battle of Jalandhar (1298) was the first major Mongol engagement under Alauddin — it must come first.
The Battle of Kili (1299) followed Jalandhar, featuring Zafar Khan's heroic death — second in sequence.
The Battle of Amroha (1305) came after Kili — Mongols were defeated decisively here.
The Battle of Ravi (1306) was the last major Mongol invasion repulsed by Alauddin — it must come last.
Correct sequence: Jalandhar → Kili → Amroha → Ravi = option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Kili-Jalandhar reversal is the classic temporal-swap trap. Kili is more frequently discussed because of Zafar Khan's death, making students associate it with an earlier, more foundational conflict. The lesser-known Battle of Jalandhar (1298) actually preceded Kili (1299) by one year. Students ranking by historical significance rather than chronology will place Kili first.
solution.final_explanation:
Alauddin Khilji faced a sustained Mongol threat requiring coordinated military responses. The correct sequence of major battles is:

1. Battle of Jalandhar (1298): First major Mongol invasion under Alauddin, repulsed by his generals.
2. Battle of Kili (1299): Second invasion — notable for Zafar Khan's individual charge that resulted in his death, illustrating the tension between personal heroism and disciplined strategy that Alauddin sought to institutionalise.
3. Battle of Amroha (1305): A decisive Mongol defeat under Alauddin's commanders.
4. Battle of Ravi (1306): The final major Mongol invasion attempt, comprehensively repelled — Alauddin's reformed army showed its full capability here.

Option (c) reflects this sequence correctly.

Value Addition:
• Alauddin faced at least 6 Mongol invasions — these battles were not isolated incidents but an existential military pressure that drove reforms.
• Zafar Khan's death at Kili highlighted why Alauddin thereafter discouraged individual initiative in favour of coordinated disciplined warfare.
• The success against Mongols is considered Alauddin's greatest military achievement, protecting the subcontinent from the devastation experienced by West Asia.

solution.concept_anchor: Sawar/Do-aspa/Se-aspa vs. Mansabdari — chronological distinction
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (Mansabdari system of the Mughals) is the most dangerous distractor because it describes cavalry grading, sounds functionally similar, and involves a real historical system — students with partial knowledge who know Mansabdari graded soldiers may choose it without checking the dynasty.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes a sultan of the Delhi Sultanate in the early 14th century — this rules out any Mughal-era system.
The three-tier cavalry grading based on number of horses maintained by a soldier points specifically to Alauddin's Sawar/Do-aspa/Se-aspa classification.
Eliminate option (b): Mansabdari was a Mughal system introduced by Akbar — over two centuries after the scenario's time period.
Eliminate option (a): Feudal contingent system was precisely what Alauddin REPLACED — it involved iqtadars raising troops, not individual soldiers maintaining graded horse counts.
Option (d) — Sawar, Do-aspa, Se-aspa grading system — is the correct identification.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap here is between Alauddin's cavalry grading (Sawar/Do-aspa/Se-aspa) and the Mughal Mansabdari system. Both grade cavalry by numerical classification, and both are associated with a more organised military. A student who has studied Mansabdari more recently than Alauddin's reforms may default to Mansabdari without recognising that the scenario is set in the Khilji period — approximately 250 years before Akbar.
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario describes Alauddin Khilji's systematic cavalry classification, which was a cornerstone of his military quality-control regime.

The system worked as follows:
• Sawar: soldier maintaining one horse — basic grade, lowest pay supplement
• Do-aspa: soldier maintaining two horses — intermediate grade
• Se-aspa: soldier maintaining three horses — highest grade, maximum pay

This grading required the Dagh system to be meaningful — branding verified that the claimed horses were actually owned and registered.

Option analysis:
• Option (a) — Feudal contingent: this was the pre-Alauddin system of iqtadars raising troops. Alauddin replaced this.
• Option (b) — Mansabdari: a Mughal innovation under Akbar, over two centuries later. Conceptually similar but chronologically wrong.
• Option (c) — Naqdi system: naqdi refers to the cash salary mechanism, not the cavalry grading classification.
• Option (d) — Correct: Sawar/Do-aspa/Se-aspa grading is precisely what the scenario describes.

Value Addition:
• The Do-aspa/Se-aspa concept prefigures the Mughal Mansabdari sawar rank — UPSC explicitly tests this comparative continuity.
• This grading improved shock capability against Mongol light cavalry by concentrating heavier multi-horse riders.
• Quality control through Dagh made this grading verifiable rather than self-reported.

A medieval sultan of the Delhi Sultanate introduced a system whereby cavalry soldiers were classified into three tiers based on the number of registered horses they personally maintained — one horse, two horses, or three horses — with salary supplements calibrated to each tier. The classification was enforceable only because each horse carried a permanent physical mark linking it to its registered owner-soldier. This system was designed to improve cavalry quality and concentrate heavier mounted forces.

(b) The Mansabdari system of the Mughal Empire in which cavalry obligations were determined by numerical rank
(c) The naqdi (cash salary) reform in which soldier payment was standardised across cavalry grades
(d) The Sawar, Do-aspa, and Se-aspa cavalry classification system introduced by Alauddin Khilji

solution.concept_anchor: Four ordinances — social controls targeting noble power
solution.strong_distractor: c — Prohibition of wine consumption seems like a religious injunction rather than a political control measure, making students consider it the 'odd one out' — but it was explicitly one of Alauddin's four ordinances targeting noble socialisation and cohesion.
elimination_logic: Identify the category: Alauddin's four ordinances were social-administrative controls to prevent noble rebellion by disrupting their financial and social networks.
Prohibition of social gatherings — directly disrupts noble networking — belongs to the ordinances.
Prohibition of wine consumption — disrupts social cohesion occasions (feasts where conspiracies formed) — belongs to the ordinances.
Prohibition of inter-marriage among nobles without royal permission — prevents alliance-building — belongs to the ordinances.

Requiring nobles to present military contingents on their own initiative without the Sultan's summons — this describes the OLD feudal obligation, not one of Alauddin's four ordinances — this is the odd one out.
Select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) — wine prohibition — is the strong distractor. It appears to be a religious measure rather than a political one, prompting students to classify it as outside the administrative-political category of the four ordinances. However, Barani explicitly includes it as one of the four because social gatherings over wine were precisely where noble conspiracies were hatched. Option (b) — unsummoned military contingents — is a feature of the feudal system Alauddin was dismantling, not a prohibition he introduced.
solution.final_explanation:
Alauddin's four ordinances targeted the socio-economic base of noble power. Three of the four options describe genuine components of these ordinances.

• Option (a) — Prohibition of social gatherings among nobles: Genuine ordinance. Nobles meeting informally could plan rebellions — Alauddin banned such assemblies.
• Option (b) — Nobles required to present military contingents without royal summons: This is the ODD ONE OUT. This describes the feudal obligation Alauddin was abolishing, not one of his four prohibitions.
• Option (c) — Prohibition of wine consumption: Genuine ordinance. Banquets and wine-drinking sessions were social occasions where conspiratorial alliances formed.
• Option (d) — Prohibition of inter-marriage among nobles without royal permission: Genuine ordinance. Matrimonial alliances between powerful families created rival power blocs.

Value Addition:
• Barani's Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi is the source for these four ordinances — their framing reflects Alauddin's ruthlessly political approach to governance.
• Accumulation of surplus wealth was the fourth prohibition — economic independence was the material base for potential rebellion.
• Alauddin went further than Balban's 'blood and iron' policy by targeting the social infrastructure of noble power, not just individuals.

solution.concept_anchor: Four market categories and their administrative officers

statement_analysis.statement: Alauddin Khilji's four regulated markets covered grain, cloth, cattle and horses, and slaves and animals — with price controls enforced by a Shahna (controller) stationed at each market.
statement_analysis.reason: These are the four markets described by Barani, and the Shahna (also called Shahai) was the controller posted at each market to enforce prices, with a Barid (intelligence officer) providing surveillance.

statement_analysis.statement: When Alauddin's successor Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah dismantled market price controls, the military salary structure remained unaffected because Alauddin had separately endowed a permanent military fund.
statement_analysis.reason: No permanent military endowment fund was established. The deregulation of markets directly undermined the purchasing power of the low nominal salaries, causing the army's sustainability to collapse — there was no separate buffer fund.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Both correct — tempts students who know Statement 1 is accurate and may not know enough about the post-Alauddin fiscal arrangements to identify Statement 2's false claim about a 'permanent military fund.'
elimination_logic: Statement 1: The four market categories (grain, cloth, cattle/horses, slaves/animals) and the Shahna as controller are historically documented — accept as correct.

Statement 2: The claim of a 'permanent military fund' separately endowed by Alauddin is a plausible-fabrication — no such fund existed; the collapse after Alauddin's death is well-documented as a direct consequence of market deregulation.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 introduces a 'permanent military fund' — a plausible-fabrication designed to sound like prudent statecraft. A student who knows Alauddin was a sophisticated administrator might accept that he would have created such a buffer. The trap is that the entire system's genius — and fragility — was its real-time interdependence with price controls, not any reserve fund.
solution.final_explanation:
Alauddin's market reform was an administrative masterpiece with significant limitations. Understanding both is essential.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The four markets (grain/cloth/cattle+horses/slaves+animals) were each controlled by a Shahna enforcing prices and a Barid (intelligence officer) reporting violations. The administrative machinery was elaborate and effective during Alauddin's lifetime.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: No separate military endowment fund existed. The system's entire logic depended on real-time price suppression — when Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah freed market prices, soldiers' nominal wages became genuinely inadequate, making the large army fiscally unviable.

Value Addition:
• The Barid in each market served a dual function — market intelligence AND political surveillance of traders and noble households.
• Alauddin's market system is sometimes called the first systematic price-control regime in Indian medieval history.
• The four-market structure anticipated some features of rationing systems, with the state acting as a price-setter rather than a market participant.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Pairing Malik Kafur with the Pandya kingdom of Madurai sounds plausible because Madurai was indeed a Deccan-south India target, but students may confuse whether the Pandya kingdom or the Hoysala kingdom (Dwarsamudra) was specifically associated with the southernmost campaign.
elimination_logic: Malik Kafur's campaigns are well-sequenced: Devagiri (1307), Warangal (1309-10), Dwarsamudra/Hoysalas (1310-11), Madurai/Pandyas (1311).
Eliminate option (b): Warangal was ruled by the Kakatiyas, not the Yadavas — Devagiri was the Yadava kingdom.
Eliminate option (c): Madurai's ruling dynasty was the Pandyas — this sounds correct, BUT the option pairs Kafur with Madurai as his FIRST campaign — his first campaign was against Devagiri.
Eliminate option (d): Dwarsamudra was the capital of the Hoysalas, not the Kakatiyas — Kakatiyas were at Warangal.
Option (a) — Devagiri as the Yadava kingdom targeted in Kafur's first Deccan campaign — is correctly matched.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Entity-swap between kingdoms and capitals/dynasties is the trap here. Options (b) and (d) swap the Yadava/Kakatiya association. Option (c) pairs Madurai correctly with Pandyas but introduces a false sequencing implication. Students who know Kafur reached Madurai but are uncertain about the first campaign target may select (c) or (d).
solution.final_explanation:
Malik Kafur's Deccan campaigns between 1307 and 1311 demonstrated the reach and effectiveness of Alauddin's reformed army.

• Option (a) — Correct: Devagiri (modern Daulatabad) was the capital of the Yadava kingdom — Kafur's first Deccan campaign target in 1307. This pair is accurately matched.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Warangal was the Kakatiya capital, not the Yadava — the Yadavas ruled from Devagiri. Entity-swap between two Deccan kingdoms.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: While Madurai was indeed the Pandya stronghold, this option incorrectly implies it was Kafur's first campaign. Madurai was the final and southernmost campaign (1311).
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Dwarsamudra was the Hoysala capital, not the Kakatiya capital. Kakatiyas were at Warangal — another entity-swap.

Value Addition:
• The campaign sequence Devagiri → Warangal → Dwarsamudra → Madurai is a recurring UPSC factual sequence.
• The Kohinoor diamond is sometimes associated with Alauddin's Deccan haul — though its precise provenance is debated by historians.
• Malik Kafur was a 'military slave' (purchased by Alauddin's general Nusrat Khan) — his identity as a eunuch-commander is frequently tested.

solution.concept_anchor: Siri fort — purpose, location, and distinctness

statement_analysis.statement: Siri was constructed by Alauddin Khilji as a garrison city separate from the older city of Delhi (Lal Kot/Qila Rai Pithora), intended primarily to house and quarter his expanded standing army.
statement_analysis.reason: Siri was indeed built as a new settlement to accommodate the large permanent army — it was distinct from the earlier settlement around the Qutb complex in Mehrauli.

statement_analysis.statement: The Tughlaqabad fort, built by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, was constructed on the same site as Siri, expanding and reinforcing Alauddin's original fortifications.
statement_analysis.reason: Tughlaqabad was a separate fort city built by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq at a different location — it was NOT built on the same site as Siri. These are distinct architectural-military complexes.

statement_analysis.statement: Alauddin's fortification strategy integrated physical garrison towns with the deployment requirements of his centrally recruited standing army, creating a strategic relationship between fort-building and military reform.
statement_analysis.reason: The garrison towns served as deployment bases for the standing army — fort-building and the standing army reform were two complementary dimensions of the same defensive strategy.

solution.strong_distractor: b — 2 and 3 only — tempts students who are uncertain about Statement 1's specific claim that Siri was separate from old Delhi, potentially misidentifying it with the Qutb complex area.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Siri was a new garrison city distinct from old Delhi settlements — this is accurate. Accept.
Statement 2: Tughlaqabad was built by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq at a DIFFERENT location from Siri — the claim of 'same site' is false. Eliminate.
Statement 3: Fort-building and standing army deployment were integrated strategic dimensions — this is accurate. Accept.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option (d): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap in Statement 2 conflates Siri and Tughlaqabad — both are medieval fort cities near Delhi built in roughly the same era, making the confusion plausible. Students who have studied the 'Seven Cities of Delhi' framework may incorrectly associate successive fort cities as built on the same site when they were actually distinct locations.
solution.final_explanation:
Alauddin's fortification policy was an architectural extension of his military strategy, not merely a construction programme.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Siri was the second city of Delhi (after Qila Rai Pithora in Mehrauli) and was specifically designed as a garrison settlement — distinct from the older Qutb complex area in Mehrauli.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Tughlaqabad was built by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq (r. 1320–25) at a separate, more southeasterly location from Siri. These represent two of the 'Seven Cities of Delhi' — distinct in location, builder, and purpose.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The strategic integration of garrison towns with the standing army's deployment needs was deliberate — Siri housed soldiers who could be rapidly mobilised against Mongol incursions from the northwest.

Value Addition:
• The Seven Cities of Delhi: Qila Rai Pithora → Siri → Tughlaqabad → Jahanpanah → Firozabad → Dinpanah/Purana Qila → Shahjahanabad — a popular UPSC sequence question.
• Jahanpanah was built by Muhammad bin Tughlaq to connect Siri and Qila Rai Pithora.
• Siri's fortifications were reportedly built partly using the labour of captive Mongol soldiers after the 1299 invasion.

solution.concept_anchor: Centralisation of military appointments and succession crisis

statement_analysis.statement: Alauddin's personal control over all high military appointments was a policy of mere despotism with no strategic rationale, driven by personal insecurity rather than a response to noble rebellions.
statement_analysis.reason: The centralisation of military appointments was directly triggered by specific noble rebellions — including Malik Chhajju's revolt and the Gujarat revolt — making it a strategic necessity, not mere despotism.

statement_analysis.statement: Firuz Shah Tughlaq's re-empowerment of nobles with hereditary military roles represented a direct reversal of the centralisation model Alauddin had established.
statement_analysis.reason: Firuz Shah restored hereditary military service and jagirs — the exact mechanisms Alauddin had dismantled — making his reign a documented reversal of Alauddin's centralisation model.

statement_analysis.statement: Alauddin's over-centralisation of military command meant that no institutional military leadership structure outlasted him, contributing to the rapid succession crisis that followed his death.
statement_analysis.reason: Because military appointments depended entirely on Alauddin's personal patronage, the institutional framework collapsed without his presence — a recognised consequence of over-centralisation noted by historians.

solution.strong_distractor: d — None incorrect (i.e., all correct) — tempts students who know Statements 2 and 3 are correct and partially accept Statement 1's claim that the policy had elements of personal insecurity, which is superficially not entirely wrong.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: The key phrase 'no strategic rationale, driven by personal insecurity rather than a response to noble rebellions' makes this incorrect — specific rebellions (Malik Chhajju, Gujarat revolt) are historically documented catalysts.
Statement 2: Firuz Shah's restoration of hereditary military service is well-documented — this is correct.
Statement 3: The succession crisis after Alauddin's death is attributed partly to over-centralisation — this is correct.
Only Statement 1 is NOT correct → option (a): 1 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 uses a partial-truth trap: Alauddin's centralisation DID have elements that could be called autocratic, and some historians do note personal dimensions to his policy. But the statement goes further by denying ANY strategic rationale — a false claim. Students who are uncomfortable defending Alauddin against the 'despot' label may not catch that the question asks what is NOT correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Alauddin's military centralisation must be understood in its historical context — as a response to real threats, not merely an expression of personal character.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect (the NOT correct statement): Noble rebellions — Malik Chhajju in 1291 and the Gujarat revolt — were concrete strategic triggers for centralising military appointments. The claim of 'no strategic rationale' is demonstrably false.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Firuz Shah Tughlaq (r. 1351–88) explicitly restored hereditary military service and jagir assignments — the key reversals of Alauddin's model, documented in the Futuhat-i-Firuz Shahi.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Historians widely note that personalised military systems — where all authority flows from one individual — collapse when that individual is removed. Alauddin's successors faced exactly this institutional vacuum.

Value Addition:
• Malik Chhajju's rebellion (1291) predated Alauddin's reign but shaped his approach to noble power once he became Sultan.
• The contrast between Alauddin's and Firuz Shah's military policies is a recurring comparative question in UPSC Mains.
• Barani both admired Alauddin's efficiency and lamented what he saw as the social degradation of his administrative model.

solution.concept_anchor: Infantry composition, pay, and tactical role in Alauddin's army

statement_analysis.statement: Infantry soldiers (paidal) in Alauddin's army were paid at a lower rate than cavalry soldiers, reflecting the differential value assigned to different arms of service.
statement_analysis.reason: Infantry received approximately 78 tankas/year versus cavalry's 234 tankas/year — the differential is documented in Barani's account of the salary reform.

statement_analysis.statement: Alauddin's military reforms focused exclusively on cavalry, as infantry was considered tactically irrelevant against Mongol light cavalry and was therefore not significantly expanded.
statement_analysis.reason: Infantry was significantly expanded under Alauddin and played essential roles in siege operations, garrison duty, and logistics — the emphasis on cavalry does not imply neglect of infantry.

statement_analysis.statement: Infantry formations equipped with archery and pike weapons complemented cavalry in Alauddin's defensive strategy against Mongol incursions.
statement_analysis.reason: Infantry archers and pike-bearers provided defensive depth in engagements — the Mongol threat required combined-arms responses, not cavalry alone.

statement_analysis.statement: The infantry's low pay relative to cavalry meant that infantry soldiers were not covered by the Chehra (descriptive roll) system, which applied only to cavalry.
statement_analysis.reason: The Chehra system applied to all soldiers in the standing army to prevent 'dead pay' fraud — there is no evidence it was restricted to cavalry; its administrative logic applied universally across arms.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Only three correct — tempts students who correctly identify Statements 1, 2, and 3's verdicts but may not independently evaluate Statement 4's false claim about Chehra's scope.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Infantry at lower pay than cavalry — confirmed by Barani's salary figures. Correct.
Statement 2: 'Focused exclusively on cavalry' is the scope-extension trap — infantry was expanded and tactically deployed. Incorrect.
Statement 3: Combined-arms use of infantry archers/pike-bearers against Mongols is historically consistent. Correct.
Statement 4: Chehra as cavalry-only is an unsupported fabrication — it was an army-wide anti-fraud measure. Incorrect.
Two statements (1 and 3) are correct → option (b): Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the known emphasis on cavalry to suggest infantry was neglected — a scope-extension that takes a true fact (cavalry was prioritised) and falsely extends it to exclusivity. Statement 4 creates a plausible-sounding administrative refinement (Chehra for cavalry only, matching the pay emphasis) that has no historical basis.
solution.final_explanation:
Infantry tends to be underappreciated in discussions of Alauddin's military because of the celebrated cavalry classification system, but the paidal (foot soldier) force was integral to his military architecture.

• Statement 1 — Correct: ~78 tankas/year for infantry vs ~234 tankas/year for cavalry — the threefold differential reflected the capital cost of horse maintenance, not disregard for infantry.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The scope-extension 'focused exclusively on cavalry' is false. Infantry performed siege operations (critical in Deccan campaigns), garrison duty in border forts, and logistical support — all indispensable functions.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Infantry archers could engage Mongol cavalry at range while pike formations disrupted mounted charges — combined arms was the actual tactical model.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: The Chehra system was a universal army anti-fraud mechanism, not cavalry-specific. Restricting it to cavalry would leave infantry 'dead pay' fraud unaddressed — contradicting the system's purpose.

Value Addition:
• Sieges of Deccan fortresses like Devagiri and Warangal required infantry expertise — cavalry alone could not conduct sieges.
• Alauddin's army composition (infantry + cavalry + war elephants) represented combined-arms doctrine ahead of its time in the subcontinent.
• The infantry's garrison role in Siri and border forts integrated the fortification policy with the standing army reform.

solution.concept_anchor: Historical sources on Alauddin — authors, works, and biases
solution.strong_distractor: a — This option pairs Amir Khusrau with Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi, which sounds plausible because Khusrau was a prolific literary figure whose works could sound like a chronicle — students confuse the chronicle title with Khusrau's works.
elimination_logic: Anchor the clearest match: Ziauddin Barani wrote Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi — match A with 3.
Amir Khusrau wrote Khaza'in-ul-Futuh (Treasures of Victory), a laudatory account of Alauddin — match B with 1.
Archaeological evidence from Siri fort remains serves as a corrective to textual bias — match C with 4.

The characteristic of writing decades after events with possible bias against 'low-born' reforms applies to Barani's methodology — but since A is already matched, match D (hagiographic/laudatory bias) with 2 (Amir Khusrau).

Wait — re-examine: D describes 'laudatory, written during Alauddin's reign' — this is Khusrau. C describes 'physical remains as corrective' — this is archaeological. B is Khusrau's work. Correct matching: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap pairs Amir Khusrau with Barani's chronicle title or vice versa. Khusrau was a poet-historian and Barani was a prose chronicler — students who know both names but not their specific works may swap the title-to-author association. The bias descriptions in List II also require careful matching: Barani's bias was retrospective and potentially against Alauddin's social policies; Khusrau's bias was contemporaneous and flattering.
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding medieval historical sources requires knowing not just what they say but who wrote them, when, and with what agenda.

Correct matches:
• A (Ziauddin Barani) — 3 (Author of Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi, wrote during Firuz Shah's reign): Barani wrote retrospectively, decades after Alauddin, with potential bias against reforms that elevated 'low-born' officials.
• B (Amir Khusrau) — 1 (Author of Khaza'in-ul-Futuh, a near-contemporary account): Khusrau's 'Treasures of Victory' is a laudatory text written during Alauddin's reign — valuable for contemporaneity but limited by hagiographic enthusiasm.
• C (Siri fort archaeological remains) — 4 (Physical evidence that acts as a corrective to textual sources): Material remains provide independent verification where textual sources may exaggerate or omit.
• D (Hagiographic/laudatory bias, writing during Alauddin's reign) — 2 (Characteristic of Amir Khusrau's historical works): Khusrau's court-poet status made flattery structurally inevitable.

Value Addition:
• Barani's Fatawa-i-Jahandari is another important work — a treatise on statecraft rather than a chronicle.
• Source criticism is increasingly tested in UPSC Mains — the 'what and why' of medieval historiography matters as much as the events themselves.
• Coin hoards from Alauddin's period confirm the monetisation implied by the naqdi salary system, corroborating textual accounts.

solution.concept_anchor: Barids and munhiyans — dual political and military espionage functions
solution.strong_distractor: b — Both correct but R not explaining A — tempts students who know the spy system had both political and military dimensions and may question whether one explains the other without carefully examining the causal logic.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Alauddin's barids and munhiyans monitored both nobles (political) and military rolls (corruption) — A is factually correct.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — The four ordinances (social gatherings, wine, inter-marriage, surplus wealth) were indeed designed to disrupt noble power networks — R is factually correct.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — The four ordinances created a regulatory framework that required surveillance to enforce — the spy system (A) was the enforcement mechanism for the ordinances (R). R explains why a comprehensive spy network was institutionally necessary, making R the correct explanation of A.
A correct + R correct + R explains A → option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
Alauddin's spy network and his four ordinances were two halves of the same governance architecture — the ordinances created prohibitions; the spies enforced them.

Assertion (A): Alauddin deployed barids (intelligence couriers) and munhiyans (secret informants) to monitor noble conduct and detect corruption in military rolls. This dual function — political surveillance of nobles AND military integrity monitoring — is historically documented. A is correct.

Reason (R): The four ordinances prohibited social gatherings, wine consumption, inter-noble marriages, and surplus wealth accumulation. Without active surveillance, these prohibitions would have been unenforceable — nobles could simply conduct prohibited activities in private. R is correct.

Causal link: R explains A because the four ordinances (R) necessitated the comprehensive spy network (A). The prohibitions were meaningless without enforcement intelligence. This is a genuine causal relationship: ordinances → need for surveillance → barids and munhiyans.

Correct answer: (a) — Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A.

Value Addition:
• Chandragupta Maurya's intelligence network (described in Arthashastra) is UPSC's favourite cross-period comparison for Alauddin's spy system.
• Munhiyans were embedded informants, while barids were reporting officers — a distinction that occasionally appears in questions.
• The espionage network also monitored market prices, making it integral to the market reform enforcement as well.

solution.concept_anchor: Do-aspa/Se-aspa vs. Mansabdari — chronological and conceptual distinction

statement_analysis.statement: Alauddin Khilji's cavalry classification into Sawar (one horse), Do-aspa (two horses), and Se-aspa (three horses) grades prefigured the sawar rank within the Mughal Mansabdari system, though the two systems were separated by over two centuries.
statement_analysis.reason: The conceptual parallel between Alauddin's horse-count grading and the Mughal Mansabdari sawar rank is recognised by historians as a precedent relationship — though Akbar's Mansabdari (late 16th century) post-dated Alauddin's system (early 14th century) by approximately 250 years.

statement_analysis.statement: Alauddin's Do-aspa and Se-aspa grades were essentially the same system as the Mughal Mansabdari, with Akbar merely renaming and formalising what Alauddin had already established.
statement_analysis.reason: While conceptually similar in grading cavalry by horse count, the Mansabdari was a comprehensive numerical ranking system governing all aspects of noble obligation, salary, and status — far more elaborate than Alauddin's horse-based cavalry grading, which was narrowly focused on military quality control.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Both correct — students who know the parallel between Do-aspa/Se-aspa and Mansabdari is historically noted may accept Statement 2 as a legitimate description of that parallel without catching the 'essentially the same system' conflation.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: The prefiguring relationship between Do-aspa/Se-aspa and Mansabdari sawar rank is historically acknowledged — with the critical caveat of 250 years of separation. The statement includes that caveat, making it correct.

Statement 2: 'Essentially the same system' and 'merely renaming' are false — Mansabdari was a comprehensive ranking governing nobility, not just cavalry grading. The scope and function were different. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap in Statement 2 collapses the 250-year gap between Alauddin's cavalry classification and Akbar's Mansabdari. The systems share a conceptual ancestor-descendant relationship, but 'essentially the same system' erases the enormous administrative elaboration that occurred over two and a half centuries. Students who know the comparative angle may overcorrect and treat the similarity as identity.
solution.final_explanation:
The Alauddin-Mansabdari comparison is a favourite UPSC cross-period question that tests nuanced understanding of continuity versus transformation.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Do-aspa/Se-aspa classification did influence later cavalry grading concepts, and the Mansabdari sawar rank bears conceptual resemblance. The statement correctly acknowledges the 250-year gap, making it a careful and accurate claim.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Mansabdari was not a rename of Alauddin's system. Akbar's Mansabdari governed the entire Mughal nobility — their rank, obligations, salary, and status — using a dual zat (personal rank) and sawar (cavalry obligation) structure. Alauddin's system was narrowly military, focused only on horse count per cavalry soldier.

Value Addition:
• Mansabdari was introduced by Akbar around 1571–72, approximately 260 years after Alauddin's reforms.
• The Zat rank in Mansabdari had no parallel in Alauddin's system — it governed personal nobility, not cavalry grade.
• The Do-aspa/Se-aspa → Mansabdari sawar lineage is a cross-period intellectual exercise, not a direct institutional inheritance.

solution.concept_anchor: Diwan-i-Arz vs. Diwan-i-Wizarat — distinct mandates
solution.strong_distractor: a — Diwan-i-Wizarat is the strongest distractor because it was the other major department that interacted closely with the military salary reform through treasury operations, making students conflate the two.
elimination_logic: The blank requires the military department that handled soldier recruitment, muster rolls, and pay.
Eliminate option (a): Diwan-i-Wizarat was the finance/revenue department — not the military recruitment department.
Eliminate option (b): Diwan-i-Insha handled royal correspondence and decrees — no military personnel function.
Eliminate option (d): Diwan-i-Rasalat handled religious and diplomatic correspondence — unrelated to military administration.
Option (c): Diwan-i-Arz was the military department responsible for recruitment, muster (including Dagh and Chehra), and pay — correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Diwan-i-Wizarat is the trap because the salary reform required close coordination between the military department and the treasury. Students who know Alauddin's cash salary reform was fiscally sophisticated may associate it with the finance department rather than recognising that Diwan-i-Arz held the administrative military function while Diwan-i-Wizarat managed the treasury from which funds flowed.
solution.final_explanation:
The four major departments of the Delhi Sultanate had distinct, non-overlapping mandates.

• Option (a) — Diwan-i-Wizarat: Incorrect. This was the revenue and finance department headed by the Wazir — it managed the treasury from which military salaries were paid but did not recruit, muster, or administer soldiers.
• Option (b) — Diwan-i-Insha: Incorrect. This department handled royal letters, decrees, and correspondence — purely administrative/clerical.
• Option (c) — Diwan-i-Arz: Correct. The military department headed by the Ariz-i-Mumalik that was empowered by Alauddin to implement Dagh and Chehra, conduct musters, and manage soldier pay.
• Option (d) — Diwan-i-Rasalat: Incorrect. This handled religious endowments and foreign/diplomatic correspondence.

Value Addition:
• Alauddin reportedly reviewed muster rolls from Diwan-i-Arz personally — an exceptional degree of sultanic involvement in departmental affairs.

solution.concept_anchor: Strategic context of military reforms — Mongol existential threat
solution.strong_distractor: c — 'To consolidate newly acquired Deccan territories' is deceptive because Alauddin DID conduct Deccan campaigns and the army was used there — but the PRIMARY driver of his comprehensive military overhaul was the northwest Mongol threat, not Deccan consolidation.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): suppressing internal trade guild revolts is not historically documented as a driver of military reform — plausible-fabrication.
Eliminate option (c): Deccan consolidation was a USE of the reformed army, not the primary catalyst for the reforms themselves.
Eliminate option (d): diplomatic rivalry with the Ilkhanate is a fabrication — the Mongol threat was military, not primarily diplomatic.
Confirm option (b): Alauddin faced at least 6 major Mongol invasions — this existential threat from the northwest was the dominant strategic context for military reorganisation.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) exploits the known connection between Alauddin and the Deccan campaigns. Students who associate Malik Kafur's campaigns with the need for a powerful army may conclude that Deccan consolidation drove the reforms. The key distinction is that the reforms preceded the Deccan campaigns and were primarily reactive to the Mongol threat — the Deccan campaigns were an offensive outcome of a defensively motivated military modernisation.
solution.final_explanation:
Alauddin's military reforms are sometimes presented as administrative innovations in isolation — but their strategic context is equally important for UPSC.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: No documented trade guild revolts served as the catalyst — this is a plausible-fabrication using plausible medieval terminology.
• Option (b) — Correct: Alauddin faced at least six major Mongol invasions. The battles of Jalandhar, Kili, Amroha, and Ravi reflect sustained existential pressure from the northwest — this is the primary documented catalyst for comprehensive military reform.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Deccan campaigns (1307–11) came AFTER the major Mongol confrontations and were enabled by the reformed army, not its primary cause.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Diplomatic rivalry with the Ilkhanate is a fabrication — the Mongol-Delhi relationship was predominantly military, not diplomatic in the relevant period.

Value Addition:
• The Mongol threat was existential — West Asia had already been devastated. Alauddin understood that a larger, disciplined, and regularly paid army was the only defence.
• Zafar Khan's death at the Battle of Kili demonstrated the cost of undisciplined individual initiative — shaping Alauddin's preference for coordinated formations.
• The northwest frontier's Mongol pressure directly explains why Siri was built as a garrison city rather than a ceremonial capital.

solution.concept_anchor: Muhammad bin Tughlaq — army without price controls, fiscal crisis

statement_analysis.statement: Muhammad bin Tughlaq attempted to maintain a large army comparable in scale to Alauddin's, but without re-establishing market price controls, the low-salary model became fiscally unsustainable.
statement_analysis.reason: Without Alauddin's market controls to keep commodity prices low, the same nominal salaries no longer provided adequate real purchasing power, creating a fiscal-military crisis under Muhammad bin Tughlaq.

statement_analysis.statement: Firuz Shah Tughlaq strengthened the centralised military appointment system inherited from Alauddin and extended it to create a more disciplined army with no hereditary privileges.
statement_analysis.reason: Firuz Shah Tughlaq did the opposite — he restored hereditary military service and jagir assignments, directly reversing Alauddin's centralisation model.

statement_analysis.statement: The Mughal Mansabdari system's sawar rank bears a conceptual resemblance to Alauddin's Do-aspa/Se-aspa cavalry grading, suggesting an evolutionary continuity in Indian cavalry organisation.
statement_analysis.reason: Historians recognise the conceptual parallel between Alauddin's horse-count grading and the Mansabdari sawar rank — an evolutionary rather than identical institutional relationship.

solution.strong_distractor: d — all three correct — tempts students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 3 as accurate and may not catch Statement 2's reversal (Firuz Shah 'strengthened' instead of 'dismantled' centralisation).
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Muhammad bin Tughlaq maintained army size without price controls — fiscal crisis is historically documented. Correct.
Statement 2: 'Firuz Shah strengthened centralised appointments and extended them with no hereditary privileges' — the opposite occurred. Firuz Shah restored hereditary military service. Incorrect.
Statement 3: Do-aspa/Se-aspa prefiguring Mansabdari sawar is a recognised historical parallel. Correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option (b): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2's partial-truth trap lies in calling Firuz Shah's policy 'strengthened centralised appointments.' Firuz Shah was indeed a strong administrator, and students who associate strong administration with centralisation may miss that his specific military policy was DECENTRALISING — restoring hereditary rights and local autonomy that Alauddin had dismantled.
solution.final_explanation:
Alauddin's reforms created a template that successors either failed to replicate or actively reversed.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Muhammad bin Tughlaq's ambitious military schemes (token currency, Deccan capital transfer) are partly explained by the fiscal squeeze of maintaining a large army without the price control subsidy that made Alauddin's low salaries viable.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Firuz Shah Tughlaq (r. 1351–88) restored hereditary military service, allowed soldiers to send sons as substitutes, and reinstated jagir-based remuneration — a comprehensive reversal of Alauddin's model, not an extension of it.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The evolutionary link between Do-aspa/Se-aspa and Mansabdari sawar is a standard UPSC comparative point — conceptual continuity over institutional transformation.

Value Addition:
• Firuz Shah's hereditary military policy is documented in his autobiography Futuhat-i-Firuz Shahi — a primary source for this reversal.
• Muhammad bin Tughlaq's token currency experiment (brass/copper for silver) was partly a failed attempt to solve the fiscal problem of maintaining large forces.
• The Alauddin-Firuz Shah contrast illustrates how medieval Indian military reforms were heavily personality-dependent rather than institutionally anchored.

solution.concept_anchor: Malik Kafur — commander illustrating reform outcomes, not reformer
solution.strong_distractor: b — Describing Kafur as the architect of military reforms tempts students who associate him strongly with Alauddin's military success and may conflate his operational role with the administrative reforms that made his campaigns possible.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes a commander executing long-distance offensive campaigns successfully — the question is what this demonstrates.
Eliminate option (a): the scenario shows operational success, not the initial design phase of military reforms — Kafur illustrated outcomes, not origins.
Eliminate option (b): Kafur was an executioner of military policy, not its architect — the reforms preceded him.
Eliminate option (d): the Mongol battles were defensive successes by Alauddin's generals including Ulugh Khan and Zafar Khan — Kafur's Deccan campaigns were offensive in character.
Option (c) — Kafur's campaigns demonstrated the offensive reach of Alauddin's reformed army — is the correct analytical mapping.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) — Kafur as architect of military reforms — is the entity-swap trap that substitutes the beneficiary of reforms for their designer. Kafur was purchased as a slave by Nusrat Khan, rose through military ranks under Alauddin's reformed system, and then commanded its most spectacular campaigns. His personal biography is often conflated with administrative reform authorship.
solution.final_explanation:
Malik Kafur's campaigns are best understood as proof-of-concept for Alauddin's military reforms, not as an independent administrative achievement.

The scenario describes: a military commander executing four major campaigns across vast distances, penetrating deep into south India — Devagiri, Warangal, Dwarsamudra, Madurai.

Option analysis:
• Option (a) — 'The initial design of military reforms': Incorrect. Reforms were designed before Kafur's prominence. The scenario describes their APPLICATION, not their design.
• Option (b) — 'Kafur as architect of reforms': Incorrect. Entity-swap — Kafur was a field commander who benefited from and illustrated reforms designed by Alauddin's administrative apparatus.
• Option (c) — Correct: Kafur's campaigns demonstrated that Alauddin's reformed standing army could conduct sustained long-distance offensive operations — a direct proof of the reformed army's effectiveness.
• Option (d) — 'Mongol defensive battles': Incorrect. Kafur's campaigns were southward offensive operations — the Mongol battles were separate northwest defensive engagements by different commanders.

Value Addition:
• Kafur's personal status (purchased slave/eunuch) illustrates how Alauddin's reformed patronage system elevated ability over birth — consistent with the broader meritocratic dimension of his reforms.
• Spoils from the Deccan campaigns financed continued military expansion — the offensive campaigns became self-funding through captured treasure.
• Warangal's Kakatiya ruler Prataparudra initially resisted but eventually submitted, paying tribute — demonstrating the reformed army's coercive effectiveness.

solution.concept_anchor: Siri fort — distinct from other Delhi historical complexes
solution.strong_distractor: c — Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque tempts students who know it is part of the Mehrauli/Qutb complex area — the same general area as Lal Kot — and may not immediately flag it as an architectural structure rather than a fortification.
elimination_logic: Identify the category: structures associated with Alauddin Khilji's fortification and military garrison strategy.
Siri fort — built by Alauddin as a garrison city — belongs to the category.
Alai Darwaza — built by Alauddin as an addition to the Qutb complex — belongs to Alauddin's architectural programme.
Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque — built by Qutbuddin Aibak, not Alauddin — this does not belong to Alauddin's construction programme at all.
Hauz-i-Khas (reservoir) — attributed to Alauddin to supply water to Siri — belongs to Alauddin's infrastructure for his garrison city.
Select option (b) — Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque — as the odd one out.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap uses the proximity of all these structures to modern Delhi to make students hesitate. Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque is in the Qutb complex area (Mehrauli), but it was built by Qutbuddin Aibak — over a century before Alauddin. Students who know Alauddin built the Alai Darwaza (an extension of the same complex) may incorrectly associate the mosque with Alauddin as well.
solution.final_explanation:
Alauddin Khilji's construction programme was strategically and architecturally significant — but it is important to distinguish his works from those of other sultans in the same geographical area.

• Option (a) — Siri fort: Built by Alauddin as a garrison city for his expanded standing army — correctly in the category.
• Option (b) — Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque: ODD ONE OUT. Built by Qutbuddin Aibak (r. 1206–10), the first Sultan of Delhi, using materials from demolished Hindu and Jain temples. Alauddin built the Alai Darwaza as an addition to this complex, but the mosque itself predates him by over a century.
• Option (c) — Alai Darwaza: Built by Alauddin in 1311 as the southern gateway to the Qutb Minar complex — correctly attributed to Alauddin.
• Option (d) — Hauz-i-Khas reservoir: Constructed by Alauddin to supply water to Siri, demonstrating that garrison city infrastructure extended beyond fortifications.

Value Addition:
• Alai Darwaza (1311) is considered one of the earliest examples of true Islamic architecture in India — a frequent UPSC architectural question.
• Hauz-i-Khas later gave its name to the surrounding area of modern Delhi.
• The Qutb complex contains works from multiple sultans — distinguishing Aibak's, Iltutmish's, and Alauddin's contributions is essential knowledge.

solution.concept_anchor: Chehra system — bureaucratic apparatus requirement under Diwan-i-Arz
solution.strong_distractor: b — Both correct but R not explaining A — tempts students who know both facts are true but may question whether the need for bureaucracy really explains the Chehra system or whether the Chehra system explains the need for bureaucracy (reversed direction).
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Chehra maintained physical descriptions of soldiers to prevent impersonation and 'dead pay' fraud. A is factually correct.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — A robust bureaucratic apparatus under Diwan-i-Arz was indeed required to record, store, and verify descriptive rolls across a large army. R is factually correct.

Step 3: Does R explain A? — The existence of the bureaucratic apparatus (R) was the enabling condition for implementing Chehra (A). Without a functioning Diwan-i-Arz with staff to record and verify individual descriptions, Chehra could not function. R causally supports A — the system required the apparatus.
A correct + R correct + R explains A → option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
The Chehra system's effectiveness depended entirely on the administrative infrastructure available to implement it.

Assertion (A): Chehra recorded the physical description of each soldier — height, complexion, distinguishing features — to prevent two related frauds: 'dead pay' (claiming salary for soldiers who had died or deserted) and impersonation (sending a substitute to muster). A is correct.

Reason (R): Implementing Chehra across an army of potentially hundreds of thousands required dedicated officials to record descriptions, maintain files, verify identities at muster, and flag discrepancies. This required significant strengthening of the Diwan-i-Arz's administrative capacity. R is correct.

Causal link: R explains A because the entire Chehra mechanism depended on the bureaucratic capacity to record and verify individual descriptions. The system created the institutional need that R describes — they are causally linked.

Correct answer: (a).

Value Addition:
• Modern military attestation and biometric identification systems are conceptual descendants of medieval descriptive roll systems like Chehra.
• The Diwan-i-Arz under Alauddin was one of the most administratively active departments in Delhi Sultanate history.
• 'Dead pay' fraud was endemic in medieval armies worldwide — Chehra was India's systematic medieval solution to this problem.

solution.concept_anchor: Four ordinances content — correct vs. fabricated prohibitions

statement_analysis.statement: Alauddin prohibited nobles from consuming wine and intoxicants, recognising that banquets and feasts were occasions where conspiratorial alliances were formed.
statement_analysis.reason: Wine prohibition is explicitly documented by Barani as one of the four ordinances — the rationale being that social drinking occasions facilitated political conspiring among nobles.

statement_analysis.statement: Alauddin prohibited inter-marriage between noble families without prior royal sanction to prevent the formation of power alliances through matrimonial ties.
statement_analysis.reason: The inter-marriage prohibition is one of Barani's four ordinances — matrimonial alliances between powerful families were a standard medieval mechanism for building rival power blocs.

statement_analysis.statement: Alauddin prohibited nobles from acquiring agricultural lands directly, instead requiring all land revenue to flow to the imperial treasury, as part of the four ordinances.
statement_analysis.reason: The four ordinances targeted social gathering, wine, inter-marriage, and surplus wealth accumulation — not specifically agricultural land acquisition. The land revenue reforms were a separate policy, not one of the four ordinances.

statement_analysis.statement: Alauddin prohibited nobles from holding private social gatherings or assemblies at which the Sultan's officials were not present.
statement_analysis.reason: Prohibition of social gatherings (mehfils) among nobles is documented as one of the four ordinances, intended to prevent the informal networking through which rebellion was historically organised.

solution.strong_distractor: d — All four correct — tempts students who know three of the four ordinances and, upon reading Statement 3 which sounds like a logical extension of Alauddin's land revenue policies, may accept it as the fourth ordinance.
elimination_logic: Statements 1, 2, and 4 correspond to documented ordinances — wine, inter-marriage, and social gatherings. Accept all three.

Statement 3 — prohibition on agricultural land acquisition — sounds like Alauddin's revenue policy but is NOT one of Barani's four ordinances. The fourth ordinance was prohibition of surplus wealth accumulation broadly, not specifically agricultural land.
Three of four statements are correct → option (c): Only three.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a plausible-fabrication that blends Alauddin's land revenue reforms (which did restrict noble land-based autonomy) with the four ordinances framework. Students who know Alauddin curtailed nobles' economic independence may accept 'prohibition on agricultural land acquisition' as the fiscal component of the ordinances, when in fact the fourth ordinance was about surplus wealth accumulation generally, not land specifically.
solution.final_explanation:
Alauddin's four ordinances are frequently tested through inclusion of a fifth false prohibition.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Wine prohibition was Ordinance 3 — feasting and drinking occasions were conspirators' preferred forums.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Inter-marriage prohibition was Ordinance 4 — matrimonial alliances created power networks that threatened royal authority.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Agricultural land acquisition prohibition is NOT one of the four ordinances. Alauddin's land revenue reforms were a separate policy strand — the fourth ordinance concerned surplus wealth accumulation broadly.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Social gathering prohibition was Ordinance 1 — the ban on informal noble assemblies without royal oversight was foundational.

The actual four ordinances per Barani: (1) prohibition of social gatherings; (2) prohibition of wine; (3) prohibition of inter-marriage without royal permission; (4) prohibition of accumulating surplus wealth.

Value Addition:
• Barani's Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi is the only source for the 'four ordinances' as a formal set — their precise formulation depends on Barani.
• The wealth accumulation prohibition directly preceded the jagir confiscation policy — the two were complementary.
• Alauddin enforced these through his spy network (barids and munhiyans), making the ordinances and espionage system functionally inseparable.

solution.concept_anchor: Iqta system — Alauddin's curtailment vs. Firuz Shah's restoration
solution.strong_distractor: b — This option pairs 'naqdi system' with 'revenue assignment to provincial governors in lieu of salary' — which describes the iqta/jagir mechanism rather than the naqdi cash payment system, exploiting students who confuse the two.
elimination_logic: Anchor: Naqdi is unambiguously 'cash salary paid directly from the treasury' — match D with 1.
Iqta: a revenue assignment to administer a territory in exchange for military/administrative service — match A with 3.
Jagir resumption: Alauddin's systematic recall of revenue assignments from military officers matches 'conversion of revenue-based remuneration to direct treasury salaries' — match B with 4.
Hereditary military service: restoration by Firuz Shah Tughlaq matches 'reversal of Alauddin's standing army reforms' — match C with 2.
Final matching: A-3, B-4, C-2, D-1 → option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) creates the trap by pairing naqdi with the iqta definition — they are conceptual opposites (cash salary vs. revenue assignment). Students who have only partially understood the distinction between iqta-based remuneration and direct treasury payment may select option (b) or (c) without cross-checking all four pairs.
solution.final_explanation:
These four concepts represent the key institutional pillars of the shift from feudal to centralised military service under Alauddin.

Correct matches:
• A (Iqta) — 3 (Assignment of a territory's revenue to an official in exchange for administrative or military service): The foundational mechanism of Delhi Sultanate provincial administration — Alauddin curtailed its military dimension without abolishing it.
• B (Jagir resumption) — 4 (Alauddin's systematic recall of revenue assignments from military officers, converting them to direct treasury salaries): This was the policy mechanism through which Alauddin operationalised the shift from iqta-based to naqdi-based military remuneration.
• C (Hereditary military service) — 2 (Firuz Shah Tughlaq's restoration of the right to pass military obligations to sons, reversing Alauddin's service-based tenure): Documented in Futuhat-i-Firuz Shahi — the clearest institutional reversal of Alauddin's model.
• D (Naqdi) — 1 (Cash salary paid directly from the imperial treasury to individual soldiers): The operative mechanism of Alauddin's standing army reform.

Value Addition:
• The iqta-to-naqdi transition required vastly larger direct treasury reserves — funded by Deccan spoils and enhanced land revenue.
• Jagir and iqta are sometimes used interchangeably but technically differ — iqta was the Delhi Sultanate term; jagir became more common in the Mughal period.
• Firuz Shah allowed sons to inherit military positions — this undid the meritocratic dimension of Alauddin's officer selection.
